lesson.intro: Every right-triangle question on the Digital SAT comes down to three tools: the Pythagorean theorem, the two special right triangles, and the three trigonometric ratios. The test almost never asks you to evaluate a trigonometric function of a messy angle; instead it hands you a ratio, or a pair of complementary angles, and asks what follows. Learn the triples on sight, keep the ratios straight, and these questions become some of the fastest points on the section.

blocks.title: The Pythagorean theorem
blocks.body:
In a right triangle, the two sides that meet at the right angle are the \textbf{legs} and the side across from the right angle is the \textbf{hypotenuse}. The hypotenuse is always the longest side, which gives you a free sanity check on every answer.

If the legs are $a$ and $b$ and the hypotenuse is $c$, then
\[a^2+b^2=c^2.\]
Used forwards, it produces the hypotenuse from two legs. Used backwards, it produces a leg: $a^2=c^2-b^2$. Deciding which side is $c$ before you write anything is the whole game.

blocks.title: Triples worth knowing on sight
blocks.body:
$3$-$4$-$5$ \qquad $5$-$12$-$13$ \qquad $8$-$15$-$17$ \qquad $7$-$24$-$25$

Any multiple of a triple is also a right triangle: $6$-$8$-$10$, $9$-$12$-$15$, $10$-$24$-$26$, $15$-$36$-$39$. If two sides of a right triangle match a scaled triple, write the third side down without squaring anything.

blocks.title: The two special right triangles
blocks.body:
Two right triangles have side ratios you are expected to know cold, because the test uses them to avoid giving you a calculator-dependent answer.

A $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle is half a square. A $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle is half an equilateral triangle, which is why its short leg is exactly half the hypotenuse.

blocks.title: Special right triangle ratios
blocks.body:
$45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$: \quad $\text{leg} : \text{leg} : \text{hypotenuse} = x : x : x\sqrt{2}$

$30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$: \quad $\text{short leg} : \text{long leg} : \text{hypotenuse} = x : x\sqrt{3} : 2x$

In both, the shortest side faces the smallest angle. Going from a short side up to a long one you \emph{multiply}; going from a long side down to a short one you \emph{divide}.

blocks.title: SOHCAHTOA
blocks.body:
For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle,
\[\sin\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}},\qquad\cos\theta=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}},\qquad\tan\theta=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}.\]
\textbf{Opposite} and \textbf{adjacent} are read relative to the angle you named, so the same side is opposite one acute angle and adjacent to the other. The hypotenuse never changes roles.

Because a single ratio names two sides, one ratio plus the Pythagorean theorem rebuilds the entire triangle. If $\sin\theta=\frac{3}{5}$, set opposite $=3k$ and hypotenuse $=5k$; the third side is $4k$, and every other ratio follows.

blocks.title: The identity the test loves: $\sin(x^\circ)=\cos\left((90-x)^\circ\right)$
blocks.body:
The two acute angles of a right triangle add to $90^\circ$. The leg opposite one of them is the leg adjacent to the other, so
\[\sin(x^\circ)=\cos\left((90-x)^\circ\right)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\cos(x^\circ)=\sin\left((90-x)^\circ\right).\]
Two consequences drive almost every SAT question on this:
\begin{itemize}\setlength{\itemsep}{2pt}
\item If $\sin A=\cos B$ for acute angles, then $A+B=90^\circ$. A trigonometric equation becomes a \emph{linear} equation.
\item In right triangle $ABC$ with the right angle at $C$, $\sin A=\cos B$ and $\cos A=\sin B$ always---no angle measure required.
\end{itemize}
Tangent behaves differently: complementary angles have \emph{reciprocal} tangents, $\tan(x^\circ)=\dfrac{1}{\tan\left((90-x)^\circ\right)}$.

blocks.title: Four mistakes that cost real points
How to attack these fast
blocks.body:
\begin{enumerate}\setlength{\itemsep}{3pt}
\item \textbf{Mark the right angle first,} then label the hypotenuse. Everything else is a leg.
\item \textbf{Check for a triple} before reaching for the calculator. Two sides from a scaled triple give the third for free.
\item \textbf{When only a ratio is given, draw the triangle} with those two sides and find the third. Never look for an angle measure you were not given.
\item \textbf{If a sine equals a cosine, add the angles to $90$.} Do not evaluate anything.
\item \textbf{Figures are not drawn to scale,} so trust the labels, not the picture---but do trust that the longest label belongs to the hypotenuse.
\end{enumerate}

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- a ratio, backwards
blocks.body:
\textit{In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, $\tan A=\frac{5}{12}$, and $AB=26$. What is the length of $\overline{BC}$?}

$\tan A=\frac{5}{12}$ names the two legs: the leg opposite $A$ is $5k$ and the leg adjacent is $12k$. The Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse $13k$, since $5$-$12$-$13$ is a triple.

We are told the hypotenuse $AB=26$, so $13k=26$ and $k=2$. The side $\overline{BC}$ is the leg opposite $A$, so $BC=5k=\mathbf{10}$.

Notice what we never did: we never found the measure of angle $A$. The ratio alone was enough.

blocks.title: Worked example 2 --- a special triangle in disguise
blocks.body:
\textit{A ramp rises from level ground to a platform $7$ feet high, making a $30^\circ$ angle with the ground. How long is the ramp?}

The ramp, the ground and the vertical height form a right triangle. The height is opposite the $30^\circ$ angle, so it is the \emph{short leg}; the ramp is the hypotenuse.

In a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle the hypotenuse is twice the short leg, so the ramp is $2\cdot 7=\mathbf{14}$ feet.

The trap answer is $7\sqrt{3}\approx 12.1$, which is the horizontal run---the long leg---not the ramp itself. Always ask which side the question named.

blocks.title: Worked example 3 --- sine equals cosine
blocks.body:
\textit{In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $(2x+5)^\circ$ and $\sin\left((2x+5)^\circ\right)=\cos\left((3x)^\circ\right)$. What is the value of $x$?}

A sine equals a cosine exactly when the angles are complementary, so
\[(2x+5)+3x=90.\]
Then $5x+5=90$, so $5x=85$ and $x=\mathbf{17}$.

Check: the angles are $39^\circ$ and $51^\circ$, which do add to $90^\circ$. The entire trigonometric dressing collapsed into a two-line linear equation---which is exactly why this item type is worth practising until it is automatic.

problems.stem: In the right triangle shown, the two legs have lengths $6$ and $8$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
problems.solution: The hypotenuse is the side across from the right angle, so it is the $c$ in $a^2+b^2=c^2$ and the legs are $a$ and $b$. Adding the squares of the legs gives $c^2$, and the last step---the one students skip---is taking the square root.

problems.stem: A right triangle has a hypotenuse of length $13$ and one leg of length $5$. What is the length of the other leg?
problems.solution: Running the theorem backwards means subtracting, not adding: the square of a leg equals the square of the hypotenuse minus the square of the other leg. The $5$-$12$-$13$ triple appears constantly on the test.

problems.stem: The legs of a right triangle have lengths $9$ and $12$. What is the length of the hypotenuse of the triangle?
problems.solution: This is the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple multiplied by $3$. Recognising a scaled triple lets you write the answer down without squaring anything, which is exactly the time saving the test is measuring.
steps: $9=3\cdot 3$ and $12=3\cdot 4$, so the triangle is a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle scaled by $3$.

problems.stem: In a right triangle, both acute angles measure $45^\circ$ and each leg has length $7$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
problems.solution: In a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle the sides are in the ratio $1:1:\sqrt{2}$, so the hypotenuse is a leg times $\sqrt{2}$. Multiplying, never dividing, is what takes you from leg to hypotenuse.
steps: The side ratio is $x : x : x\sqrt{2}$ with $x=7$.
problems.verify:
v = sqrt(7**2 + 7**2)
result = "$7\\sqrt{2}$" if simplify(v - (7*sqrt(2))) == 0 else "MISMATCH"

problems.stem: In a right triangle, the hypotenuse has length $10$ and one of the acute angles measures $30^\circ$. What is the length of the side opposite the $30^\circ$ angle?
problems.solution: In a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle the sides are in the ratio $1:\sqrt{3}:2$, in the order short leg, long leg, hypotenuse. The shortest side always sits opposite the smallest angle, so it is half the hypotenuse.
steps: The side ratio is $x : x\sqrt{3} : 2x$ with $2x=10$.
The side opposite $30^\circ$ is the $x$ side, so it is $5$.

problems.stem: In the right triangle shown, angle $A$ is an acute angle. What is the value of $\sin A$?
problems.solution: SOH: sine is opposite over hypotenuse. The side opposite angle $A$ is the one that does not touch $A$, which here is the side of length $8$, and the hypotenuse is always the side across from the right angle.
steps: Identify the side opposite $A$: it has length $8$.
Identify the hypotenuse: it has length $17$.

problems.stem: If $\sin(x^\circ)=\frac{3}{5}$, what is the value of $\cos\left((90-x)^\circ\right)$?
problems.solution: The sine of an angle and the cosine of its complement are the same number, because in a right triangle the side opposite one acute angle is the side adjacent to the other. No angle measure is needed---the identity $\sin(x^\circ)=\cos\left((90-x)^\circ\right)$ hands you the answer.
steps: The two angles $x^\circ$ and $(90-x)^\circ$ are complementary.
For complementary angles, sine and cosine swap: $\cos\left((90-x)^\circ\right)=\sin(x^\circ)$.

problems.stem: A $26$-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall, with the base of the ladder $10$ feet from the wall on level ground. How many feet up the wall does the top of the ladder reach?
problems.solution: The ladder is the hypotenuse because it is the slanted side, opposite the right angle formed by the wall and the ground. Putting the ladder in as a leg is the single most common error in this problem type.
steps: The wall and the ground meet at a right angle, so the ladder is the hypotenuse.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, $\tan A=\frac{3}{4}$, and $AC=20$. What is the length of $\overline{BC}$?
problems.solution: TOA: tangent is opposite over adjacent, and both of those sides are legs. For angle $A$ the opposite leg is $\overline{BC}$ and the adjacent leg is $\overline{AC}$, so the tangent equation links exactly the two lengths in the question.

problems.stem: In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $60^\circ$ and the side opposite the $30^\circ$ angle has length $6$. What is the length of the side opposite the $60^\circ$ angle?
problems.solution: The long leg sits opposite the $60^\circ$ angle and equals the short leg times $\sqrt{3}$; the hypotenuse is the short leg times $2$. Mixing those two multipliers is the classic slip here.
steps: The short leg is the side opposite $30^\circ$, so $x=6$.

problems.stem: Right triangles $ABC$ and $DEF$ have right angles at $C$ and $F$, and angle $A$ is congruent to angle $D$. If $AC=6$, $BC=8$, and $DF=9$, what is the length of $\overline{EF}$?
problems.solution: Two right triangles with a pair of congruent acute angles are similar, so corresponding sides are in a constant ratio. Find the scale factor from the pair of sides you know completely, then apply it once.
steps: $\overline{AC}$ and $\overline{DF}$ correspond, so the scale factor is $\dfrac{9}{6}=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

problems.stem: In right triangle $PQR$, angle $R$ is a right angle and $\cos P=\frac{7}{25}$. What is the value of $\sin Q$?
problems.solution: Angles $P$ and $Q$ are the two acute angles of a right triangle, so they add to $90^\circ$. The side adjacent to $P$ is the side opposite $Q$, which makes $\sin Q$ and $\cos P$ the same ratio of the same two sides.

problems.stem: A vertical pole stands on level ground. The angle of elevation of the sun is $45^\circ$, and the pole's shadow is $18$ feet long. What is the height, in feet, of the pole?
problems.solution: The pole, its shadow and the sun's ray form a right triangle whose acute angles are both $45^\circ$, so it is isosceles: the height equals the shadow length. The $18\sqrt{2}$ answer is the sun's ray, not the pole.
steps: The pole and the shadow are the two legs of a right triangle.
The angle of elevation is $45^\circ$, so the other acute angle is also $45^\circ$ and the legs are equal.
The height equals the shadow: $18$ feet.

problems.stem: The legs of a right triangle have lengths $8$ and $15$. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
problems.solution: Find the missing side first, then add all three. The $8$-$15$-$17$ triple is worth memorising: it turns a two-step problem into a one-step one.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle and $\sin A=\frac{3}{5}$. What is the value of $\cos A$?
problems.solution: A ratio alone is enough to rebuild the whole triangle. Read $\sin A=\frac{3}{5}$ as opposite $=3$ and hypotenuse $=5$, get the third side from the Pythagorean theorem, then read off the cosine.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is a right angle, $AB=9$, and $BC=12$. Point $D$ lies on $\overline{AC}$ so that $\overline{BD}$ is perpendicular to $\overline{AC}$. What is the length of $\overline{BD}$?
problems.solution: The area of the triangle can be computed two ways: from the two legs, or from the hypotenuse and the altitude drawn to it. Setting those equal is faster than chasing the similar triangles.

problems.stem: The acute angles of a right triangle measure $a^\circ$ and $b^\circ$. If $\sin(a^\circ)=\frac{5}{13}$, what is the value of $\cos(b^\circ)\cdot\tan(a^\circ)$?
problems.solution: Two ideas stack here. First $a+b=90$, so $\cos(b^\circ)=\sin(a^\circ)=\frac{5}{13}$. Second, a sine of $\frac{5}{13}$ forces a $5$-$12$-$13$ triangle, so the tangent is $\frac{5}{12}$.
steps: From $\sin(a^\circ)=\frac{5}{13}$ the legs are $5$ and $12$, so $\tan(a^\circ)=\frac{5}{12}$.

problems.stem: In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $(3x+10)^\circ$ and $\sin\left((3x+10)^\circ\right)=\cos\left((x+20)^\circ\right)$. What is the value of $x$?
problems.solution: When a sine equals a cosine, the two angles are complements. Turning the trigonometric equation into the linear equation $(3x+10)+(x+20)=90$ is the whole problem.

problems.stem: An equilateral triangle has side length $12$. What is the length of an altitude of the triangle?
problems.solution: An altitude of an equilateral triangle cuts it into two $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles whose hypotenuse is a full side and whose short leg is half a side. The altitude is the long leg, so it is the short leg times $\sqrt{3}$.
steps: The altitude splits the base into two segments of length $6$.
That creates a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle with short leg $6$ and hypotenuse $12$.
The altitude is the long leg, $6\sqrt{3}$.
problems.verify:
v = sqrt(12**2 - 6**2)
result = "$6\\sqrt{3}$" if simplify(v - (6*sqrt(3))) == 0 else "MISMATCH"

problems.stem: In a right triangle, $\theta$ is an acute angle and $\tan\theta=\frac{20}{21}$. What is the value of $\sin\theta$?
problems.solution: A tangent gives you both legs, so the Pythagorean theorem gives the hypotenuse and every other ratio follows. Here $20$-$21$-$29$ is the triangle; picking $\frac{21}{29}$ means the opposite and adjacent legs were swapped.

problems.stem: A straight ramp $26$ feet long runs from level ground to a loading dock. The ramp makes an angle $\theta$ with the ground, where $\sin\theta=\frac{5}{13}$. How many feet above the ground is the top of the ramp?
problems.solution: The ramp is the hypotenuse and the height is the side opposite $\theta$, so sine is exactly the ratio that connects them. Multiplying the hypotenuse by the sine is the one step required.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle and the length of $\overline{AB}$ is twice the length of $\overline{BC}$. What is the value of $\tan A$?
problems.solution: Set $BC=1$ and $AB=2$; the triangle is forced to be a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, with $AC=\sqrt{3}$. Then $\tan A$ is opposite over adjacent, which is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, and rationalising gives $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}$. Choosing $\sqrt{3}$ means the ratio was inverted.
steps: For angle $A$, the opposite leg is $BC=1$ and the adjacent leg is $AC=\sqrt{3}$.

problems.stem: In the right triangle shown, one leg has length $20$ and the hypotenuse has length $25$. What is the length of the other leg?
problems.solution: The hypotenuse is the longest side, so it must be the $c$ in $a^2+b^2=c^2$; the missing side is found by subtracting. This is the $3$-$4$-$5$ triple scaled by $5$.

problems.stem: The hypotenuse of a $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle has length $8\sqrt{2}$. What is the length of each leg?
problems.solution: Going from hypotenuse to leg reverses the ratio, so you divide by $\sqrt{2}$ instead of multiplying. Because the hypotenuse was already written with a $\sqrt{2}$, the division is clean.
steps: The ratio is leg $:$ leg $:$ hypotenuse $=x:x:x\sqrt{2}$.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is a right angle, $AB=24$, and $BC=7$. What is the value of $\tan A$?
problems.solution: Tangent uses the two legs only, and in a right triangle at $B$ both $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{BC}$ are legs. The side opposite $A$ is $\overline{BC}$, so the hypotenuse never enters the calculation.

problems.stem: Angles $A$ and $B$ are the two acute angles of a right triangle. If $\tan A=\frac{5}{12}$, what is the value of $\tan B$?
problems.solution: What is opposite angle $A$ is adjacent to angle $B$ and vice versa, so the tangents of complementary angles are reciprocals. Answering $\frac{5}{12}$ means the identity was applied as if tangent behaved like sine and cosine.
steps: $\tan A=\frac{5}{12}$ means the leg opposite $A$ is $5$ and the leg adjacent is $12$.
Those roles swap for angle $B$: opposite $12$, adjacent $5$.

problems.stem: In a $30^\circ$-$60^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangle, the side opposite the $60^\circ$ angle has length $9\sqrt{3}$. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
problems.solution: Work back to the short leg first: the long leg is the short leg times $\sqrt{3}$, so the short leg is $9$. The hypotenuse is then twice the short leg.
steps: The long leg is $x\sqrt{3}$, so $x\sqrt{3}=9\sqrt{3}$ and $x=9$.

problems.stem: A support wire runs from the top of a vertical $24$-foot pole to a point on level ground $7$ feet from the base of the pole. What is the length, in feet, of the wire?
problems.solution: The pole and the ground are perpendicular, so the wire is the hypotenuse---the longest side. Any answer smaller than $24$ can be rejected immediately.
steps: The pole and ground form the legs: $24$ and $7$.

problems.stem: In right triangle $DEF$, angle $F$ is a right angle and $\sin D=\frac{8}{17}$. What is the value of $\cos E$?
problems.solution: Angles $D$ and $E$ are complementary, and the leg opposite $D$ is the leg adjacent to $E$. Both ratios are therefore the same leg over the same hypotenuse, so no computation is needed at all.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, $BC=9$, and $\sin A=\frac{3}{5}$. What is the length of $\overline{AB}$?
problems.solution: $\overline{BC}$ is opposite angle $A$ and $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse, so those two sides are exactly the ones sine relates. Since the unknown is in the denominator, you divide rather than multiply.

problems.stem: In a right triangle, one acute angle measures $(4x-6)^\circ$ and $\cos\left((4x-6)^\circ\right)=\sin\left((x+16)^\circ\right)$. What is the value of $x$?
problems.solution: A cosine equals a sine exactly when the two angles are complementary, so the trigonometry collapses into one linear equation. The angle expressions themselves never need to be evaluated.

problems.stem: Right triangles $ABC$ and $XYZ$ are similar, with right angles at $B$ and $Y$ and with angle $A$ corresponding to angle $X$. If $AB=8$, $BC=6$, and $XY=20$, what is the length of $\overline{XZ}$?
problems.solution: Similar triangles share every angle, so every trigonometric ratio matches; the sides just scale. Find the scale factor from the matched pair $\overline{AB}$ and $\overline{XY}$, then scale the hypotenuse.

problems.stem: A vertical flagpole $40$ feet tall casts a shadow $40\sqrt{3}$ feet long on level ground. What is the measure, in degrees, of the angle of elevation of the sun?
problems.solution: The tangent of the elevation angle is height over shadow, which here is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$---the tangent of $30^\circ$. Answering $60$ means the two legs were used in the wrong order.
steps: The short leg is opposite the smallest angle, and $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$.
So the angle of elevation is $30^\circ$.
problems.verify:
t = symbols('t')
result = [s for s in solve(tan(t*pi/180) - 1/sqrt(3), t) if 0 < s < 90][0]

problems.stem: The legs of a right triangle have lengths $10$ and $24$. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
problems.solution: This is the $5$-$12$-$13$ triple doubled, so the hypotenuse is $26$ without any squaring. The question then only asks for a sum, but you cannot answer it until the third side exists.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $B$ is a right angle and $\cos A=\frac{5}{13}$. What is the value of $\tan A$?
problems.solution: One ratio determines the triangle: $\cos A=\frac{5}{13}$ gives adjacent $5$ and hypotenuse $13$, so the opposite leg is $12$. Tangent is then opposite over adjacent, and putting them the other way round produces $\frac{5}{12}$.

problems.stem: A square has a diagonal of length $10$. What is the area of the square?
problems.solution: A diagonal cuts the square into two $45^\circ$-$45^\circ$-$90^\circ$ triangles, so the side is $\frac{10}{\sqrt{2}}=5\sqrt{2}$ and the area is the side squared. Squaring the diagonal instead gives $100$.
steps: The diagonal is side $\times\sqrt{2}$, so $s\sqrt{2}=10$ and $s=5\sqrt{2}$.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, angle $A$ measures $30^\circ$, and $AC=12$. What is the length of $\overline{BC}$?
problems.solution: $\overline{AC}$ is the long leg, because it lies opposite the $60^\circ$ angle at $B$, and $\overline{BC}$ is the short leg. So $\overline{BC}$ is $\overline{AC}$ divided by $\sqrt{3}$, not multiplied by it.
steps: Angle $B=60^\circ$, so $\overline{AC}$ is the long leg and $\overline{BC}$ is the short leg.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle and $\sin A=\frac{2}{3}$. What is the value of $\cos A$?
problems.solution: The legs of a right triangle need not be integers. With opposite $=2$ and hypotenuse $=3$, the adjacent leg is $\sqrt{3^2-2^2}=\sqrt{5}$, so the cosine carries a radical. Subtracting the numerators to get $\frac{1}{3}$ is the trap.
problems.verify:
v = sqrt(1 - Rational(2,3)**2)
result = "$\\frac{\\sqrt{5}}{3}$" if simplify(v - (sqrt(5)/3)) == 0 else "MISMATCH"

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle and $\tan A=\frac{3}{4}$. The perimeter of triangle $ABC$ is $36$. What is the length of $\overline{AB}$?
problems.solution: The tangent fixes the shape but not the size, so write the sides as $3k$, $4k$ and $5k$ and let the perimeter pin down $k$. $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse because it is the side opposite the right angle at $C$.
steps: $\tan A=\frac{3}{4}$ makes the triangle a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle: legs $3k$ and $4k$, hypotenuse $5k$.

problems.stem: The acute angles of a right triangle measure $a^\circ$ and $b^\circ$. If $\cos(a^\circ)=\frac{4}{5}$, what is the value of $\dfrac{\sin(b^\circ)}{\cos(b^\circ)}$?
problems.solution: Because $a+b=90$, the identities give $\sin(b^\circ)=\cos(a^\circ)=\frac{4}{5}$ and $\cos(b^\circ)=\sin(a^\circ)=\frac{3}{5}$. The quotient of sine over cosine is the tangent, so the answer is $\tan(b^\circ)=\frac{4}{3}$; forgetting to swap gives $\frac{3}{4}$.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$ the right angle is at $C$. Point $D$ lies on $\overline{AB}$ so that $\overline{CD}$ is perpendicular to $\overline{AB}$. If $AD=4$ and $DB=9$, what is the length of $\overline{CD}$?
problems.solution: The altitude to the hypotenuse creates two triangles similar to the original and to each other, so $\frac{AD}{CD}=\frac{CD}{DB}$. That proportion makes $CD$ the geometric mean of the two pieces, not their average---which is why $\frac{13}{2}$ is offered.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle, $AB=20$, and $\sin B=\cos B$. What is the area of triangle $ABC$?
problems.solution: A sine equal to a cosine at the same angle forces that angle to be $45^\circ$, since $\sin B=\cos(90^\circ-B)$ means $B=90^\circ-B$. The triangle is therefore isosceles with legs $\frac{20}{\sqrt{2}}=10\sqrt{2}$.

problems.stem: A straight ramp $34$ feet long rises from level ground at an angle $\theta$, where $\sin\theta=\frac{8}{17}$. What is the horizontal distance, in feet, covered by the ramp?
problems.solution: Sine gives the rise, but the question asks for the run, so you need cosine. The $8$-$15$-$17$ triple turns $\sin\theta=\frac{8}{17}$ into $\cos\theta=\frac{15}{17}$ instantly; $16$ is the rise, offered for anyone who answers the wrong question.

problems.stem: In right triangle $ABC$, angle $C$ is a right angle and the measure of angle $A$ is twice the measure of angle $B$. What is the value of $\dfrac{AC}{AB}$?
problems.solution: The acute angles are complementary, so $2B+B=90$ and $B=30^\circ$. $\overline{AC}$ is the leg opposite $B$ and $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse, so the ratio is $\sin B=\sin 30^\circ=\frac{1}{2}$; reading it as $\sin A$ instead gives $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.
steps: $\overline{AC}$ is opposite angle $B$ and $\overline{AB}$ is the hypotenuse, so $\dfrac{AC}{AB}=\sin B$.
problems.verify:
b = symbols('b')
B = solve(3*b - 90, b)[0]
result = sin(B*pi/180)
